desc:
A town has n junctions numbered 0 to n - 1 and two-way roads roads[i] = [a, b, w] of length w. No two roads join the same pair of junctions.

Let d(x) be the length of the shortest route from junction x to junction n - 1 (it is infinite if there is no route). A closing-in path from 0 to n - 1 is a sequence of junctions in which consecutive junctions are joined by a road and d becomes strictly smaller at every step.

Return the number of closing-in paths modulo 1,000,000,007. For n = 1 the answer is 1 (the path consisting only of junction 0).

n = 4, roads = [[0,1,1], [1,3,1], [0,2,1], [2,3,1], [1,2,1]]
d = [2, 1, 1, 0]
paths: 0-1-3 and 0-2-3  -> 2   (1-2 is not allowed, d does not shrink)
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b < n, a ≠ b, and each pair appears at most once
hints: First you need d(x) for every junction. From which junction should you run the shortest-path search, so that one run gives all of d?
Run Dijkstra from junction n - 1. Because d must strictly decrease along a path, the paths form a DAG, so you can count them with DP instead of enumerating them.

Sort the reachable junctions by d. Set ways[n-1] = 1 and, in increasing d order, ways[u] = sum of ways[v] over roads (u, v) with d[v] < d[u]. The answer is ways[0] (0 if junction 0 cannot reach n - 1).
editorial: Roads are two-way, so distances to the target equal distances from the target: run Dijkstra from n - 1. Since weights are at least 1, n - 1 is the only junction with d = 0.

A step from u to v is allowed exactly when d[v] < d[u]. Along any allowed path d strictly decreases, so no junction repeats and the allowed steps form a directed acyclic graph that is naturally ordered by d. Count the paths from each junction to the target: ways[u] = sum(ways[v]) over allowed steps, processing junctions by increasing d so that every ways[v] is final when it is needed.

Dijkstra costs O((V + E) log V) and the DP is O(V log V + E) for the sort and the scan. Junctions with infinite d are skipped; if junction 0 is among them the answer is 0. Counts are reduced modulo 1,000,000,007 because they can be exponentially large.
